prompt.context: Your client is a leading retail bank in a South American country, with over 3,000 branches across the country. In addition to the retail business, the bank also has an Investment Banking (IB) unit, which acts as an intermediary and/or advisor when corporations want to engage in complex financial transactions (for example M&A, raising capital, initial public offering (IPO), etc.). The IB unit is headed by a Vice President who reports to the bank's CEO.
prompt.question: The IB VP hired you to evaluate whether the IB should spin off from the retail bank, becoming fully independent from the conglomerate. Should the IB unit spin off?

clarifying_info.q: What is the main motivation behind the VP's request?
clarifying_info.a: The main reason is financial — the end goal is additional profits for the IB unit.

clarifying_info.q: How do Investment Banks generate revenue?
clarifying_info.a: IBs operate on a fee-based model. They are remunerated as a percentage of the total transaction value (e.g. a 2% fee on a USD 100M transaction yields USD 2M in revenues).

clarifying_info.q: Why does the VP think the spin-off could increase revenues?
clarifying_info.a: She suspects that being attached to the retail bank prevents the IB from tapping additional revenue sources, for example through Joint Ventures with other Investment Banks.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any concerns beyond revenue?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — she is also worried about the bureaucracy imposed by the conglomerate, which slows down relevant and sometimes urgent decisions for the IB unit.

clarifying_info.q: Do we need to calculate NPV or apply a discount rate?
clarifying_info.a: For simplicity, assume no discount rate, no time value of money, and no NPV calculations are required.

clarifying_info.q: Should we consider the broader Investment Banking industry momentum?
clarifying_info.a: No — considerations regarding the momentum of the Investment Banking industry are not relevant for this case.

exhibits.title: Current and Expected Revenues by Business Line
exhibits.shows: A table with four Investment Banking business lines showing the total transaction market size, average fee percentage, current market share, and expected market share after the spin-off for each line.

footnotes: Average fee is a standard percentage of the total value of a transaction (e.g. an IPO).
Expected market share is post spin-off, as estimated by the client.
DCM market share is expected to drop because the Retail Bank cross-sells DCM deals to the IB unit, which will cease after separation.

exhibits.title: Investment Banks Cost Structure Benchmark (P&L)
exhibits.shows: A P&L summary for our client's current IB unit alongside two comparable standalone Investment Banks used as benchmarks, showing cost line items as both USD thousands and as a percentage of sales.

framework: Revenues impact: estimate incremental revenues from the change in market share across all four business lines after the spin-off
Cost impact: identify cost items that will increase because the IB currently benefits from shared services with the retail bank (e.g. IT, rent), and quantify the incremental cost
Net profit impact: subtract incremental costs from incremental revenues to determine whether the spin-off is financially beneficial
Break-even and payback: optionally assess how quickly the incremental profit covers any one-time spin-off costs (not required for this case's calculations)

Qualitative considerations: evaluate strategic, operational, and organizational implications — IB strategy, governance, legal entity, culture, organizational structure, operational model, competitive landscape, capabilities to become standalone

questions.prompt: Calculate the IB unit's current annual revenues using Exhibit 1.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the formula: Revenue = Total transaction market x Average fee x Current market share, summed across all four business lines. The fee-based revenue model should be explained if the candidate does not know it.

math.setup: Revenue per line = Total transaction market × Average fee × Market share; sum all lines.

questions.prompt: Calculate the IB unit's expected annual revenues after the spin-off using Exhibit 1.
questions.guidance: Same formula applied with the expected market shares. Candidate should note that DCM share drops (from 35% to 25%) because cross-selling from the retail bank will cease.

math.setup: Revenue per line = Total transaction market × Average fee × Expected market share; sum all lines.
math.answer: USD 25.1M in expected annual revenues — an increase of USD 6.3M (approximately one-third uplift)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, identify which cost items will change materially after the spin-off and calculate the incremental costs.
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe that IT & systems (currently 1% of revenues vs. benchmark 5–6%) and Rent & maintenance (currently 2% vs. benchmark 6–7%) are well below benchmark, likely because the IB shares these services with the retail bank. After spin-off, these should converge to benchmark levels. Front office and back office staff percentages are confirmed to remain constant.

math.setup: Incremental cost = (New % of expected revenues) − Current cost amount. Apply benchmark % to expected revenues of USD 25.1M (use USD 25M for simplicity).
steps: Current IT cost: USD 200k (1% × 18.8M); New IT cost: 5% × 25M = USD 1.25M
Current Rent cost: USD 400k (2% × 18.8M); New Rent cost: 6% × 25M = USD 1.5M

questions.prompt: What is the net profit impact of the spin-off? Is it financially worthwhile?
questions.guidance: Candidate subtracts incremental costs from incremental revenues. A clear, structured summary referencing the numbers is expected.

math.setup: Net profit impact = Incremental revenues − Incremental costs
math.answer: The spin-off generates a net profit improvement of USD 4.15M per year; financially it makes sense to proceed.

brainstorming.prompt: Aside from financial considerations, what are other pros and cons of spinning off the Investment Banking unit from the rest of the conglomerate?

categories.name: Pros
ideas: Reduced bureaucracy with no formal ties to the conglomerate, enabling faster decision-making
Greater organizational identity — the IB can build its own culture and brand
Possibility of more flexible work arrangements typical of standalone Investment Banks
Openness to engage with other institutions, for example establishing Joint Ventures with other Investment Banks

categories.name: Cons
ideas: Increased costs (IT & systems, Rent & maintenance) could end up higher than benchmarked if assumptions prove incorrect
Cross-selling with the retail bank is significantly reduced; some clients may leave the IB after the spin-off for non-mapped reasons
In the future the Retail Bank may create a new competing IB unit
Loss of strategic perspective previously provided by other areas of the bank
Limitation on talent transfer between bank divisions after separation
Legal and regulatory aspects of creating a new entity may add complexity and cost not fully modeled

recommendation: Recommend proceeding with the spin-off. The financial analysis shows a net annual profit improvement of USD 4.15M: incremental revenues of USD 6.3M driven by market share gains in ECM, M&A, and Sales & Trading outweigh incremental costs of USD 2.15M from IT and rent coming in line with industry benchmarks.
The qualitative benefits — reduced bureaucracy and the ability to pursue Joint Ventures — further support the decision.
risks: Market share gains may not materialize as estimated by the client, particularly if the IB cannot replace the cross-selling pipeline from the retail bank in DCM
Cost increases could exceed benchmark assumptions if transition costs or one-time set-up expenses are larger than expected
The retail bank could establish a new competing IB unit after separation
Talent retention risks during the transition period
next_steps: Conduct a detailed transition planning exercise covering legal entity formation, regulatory approvals, and branding
Model one-time spin-off costs (legal, IT migration, real-estate fit-out) and establish a payback period
Develop a client retention and new client acquisition strategy to ensure DCM market share does not fall further than projected
Define the standalone IB's governance structure, incentive schemes, and operational model before separation
